items.title: Learn to program using Python
items.text: This is a gentle introduction to the Python programming language. It assumes no prior programming experience and it aims to help you become fluent in the fundamentals. You will design, implement, test and debug real procedural programs, and will be able to read and reason about simple Python programs.

items.title: Learning outcomes
items.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  1. Write simple procedural programs.
  2. Read and analyze the behavior of simple programs.
  3. Apply decomposition — break a program into functions and modules.
  4. Choose appropriate data structures, conditionals, and iteration for a task.
  5. Use primitive types, variables, strings, expressions, and command-line I/O.
  6. Use conditional and iterative control structures, functions, and parameter passing.
  7. Use each of tuples, lists, sets, and dictionaries.
  8. Use the standard library.
  9. Use file I/O for persistence across runs.
  10. Test and debug simple programs.

items.title: A note on tools
items.text: You need almost nothing: a recent Python and any editor. We use the REPL (the interactive >>> prompt) constantly for quick checks, and script files for anything multi-line. The built-in help(), the official Python tutorial, and the interpreter's own error messages are the only references you will need.

items.title: Making decisions
items.text:
To be useful, programs often need to make decisions, that is, carry out certain actions based on whether certain conditions are met or not. This branching behavior stands on two legs:

  • Boolean expressions: Python expressions that produce a true or false value
  • Conditional logic: if and if-else statements. Decide whether to execute blocks of code based on the value of a boolean expression.

In this lesson we look at:

  • How to produce true or false values
  • How to test the value of a boolean expression using if statements
  • Code blocks and indentation in Python
  • How to write programs that behave differently based on input
  • More on string manipulation in Python, including string formatting

items.title: Booleans
items.text:
There are exactly two literal boolean values in Python: True and False.

However, a large number of Python expressions can evaluate to True or False.

items.title: Comparison
items.text:
Comparison operators are used to test equality (==), inequality (!=) and strict inequality (>, >=, <, <=):

>>> 3 == 3
True
>>> 3 < 3
False
>>> 5 >= 4
True
>>> 'apple' < 'banana'
True

= vs ==

= binds a variable to a value. E.g. x = 5

== compares two values for equality, return True if they are equal, and False otherwise.

Using = where == is expected is a very common error and Python will often flag it.

Comparing non-numeric values

You can compare things that are not numbers, such as strings or user-defined objects. This often requires supplying a comparison criterion or predicate.

By default, strings are compared alphabetically character by character. If you wanted to based the comparison on string length instead, then you would have to be explicit about it: len('apple') < len('banana')

items.title: Logical expressions
items.text:
You can combine multiple boolean expressions using the logical operators and, or and not to produce more complex expressions.

>>> True and True
True
>>> True and False
False
>>> True or False
True
>>> x = 3
>>> x > 0 and x <= 5
True
>>> 0 < x <= 5  # same as above
True
>>> not x > 5
True
>>> age = 25
>>> income = 40_000
>>> if age >= 18 and income > 30_000:   # BOTH must be true
...     print("eligible")
...
eligible
>>> day = "Sun"
>>> if day == "Sat" or day == "Sun":    # EITHER is enough
...     print("weekend")
...
weekend
>>> logged_in = False
>>> if not logged_in:                   # flip a boolean
...     print("please log in")
...
please log in

items.title: Truthiness
items.text:
Python allows you to use any value in conditional statements.

The following values are considered falsy:

  • zero: 0, 0.0
  • empty string
  • empty containers: [], (), {}
  • None

Everything else (non-zero numbers, non-empty strings, ...) are considered truthy.

>>> name = input("Please enter your name: ")
>>> Please enter your name: Ada
>>> if name:                                    # true if non-empty
...     print("Hi", name)
...
Ada
>>> items = []
>>> if not items:                               # same as `len(items) == 0` but cleaner
...     print("Empty")
...
Empty

items.title: Short-circuit evaluation
items.text:
Python stops evaluation logical expressions as soon as the final outcome can be determined. This allows some useful idioms:

  • Conditional execution without if statements: age < 18 and print("You are too young")
  • Default value assignment: user_name = user_input or 'Anonymous User'

  • Sentinel: guard against errors by ensuring a given operation is allowed. For example, the following code will produce an AttributeError if user is not set: 

    if not user.is_admin():
    print("Access denied")

    To prevent the AttributeError, ensure user is set:

    if user is not None and not user.is_admin():
    print("Access denied")

items.title: Other ways of getting booleans
items.text:
• is, the identity operator. Test if two variables reference the same object. Often used to test for None
  • Predicates:: functions or methods that return True or False. For example, string values have a method .isdigit() that returns True if all the characters in the string are digits, or False otherwise. Useful for testing valid user inputs. See More on strings

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
3.1 — Write sign.py that reads a number and prints positive, negative, or zero.

3.2 — Write login.py: read a username and password; grant access only if both match expected values (use and). Print distinct messages for wrong user vs. wrong password

3.3 — Write grade.py: read a score 0–100 and print the letter grade (A ≥ 90, B ≥ 80, C ≥ 70, D ≥ 60, else F). Also reject scores outside 0–100 with an error message.

3.4 — Write weekday.py: read a day name and print weekend or weekday. Accept any capitalization

3.5 — Write a program palindrome.py that prompts the user to enter a word and prints if it is a palindrome or not.

A palindrome is a word that reads the same when reversed.

Hints
  • 3.2 — nested if: outer if user == ...: then inner if password == ...:.
  • 3.4 — convert to lower case (.lower()) before comparing.
  • 3.5 — the expression [*word] converts word into a list of characters. The built-in function reversed() takes a sequence and returns its reverse. Then .join() the list of characters to form a new word.

items.title: Coding challenge — Number classifier program with a menu
items.text:
Write a menu-driven program classify.py as follows:

  1. Show a menu: 
    1) Classify a number
2) Check divisibility
3) Compare two numbers
  2. Read the user's choice with input().
  3. Branch on the choice:
  4. 1 — read a number; report whether it's positive/negative/zero and even/odd.
  5. 2 — read a number and a divisor; report whether the first is divisible by the second (n % d == 0), making sure to reject divisor 0 with an appropriate error message.
  6. 3 — read two numbers; report which is larger, or whether they're equal.
  7. If the choice isn't 1, 2, or 3, print Unknown option.
  8. Refuse to proceed on any invalid input

Exit program conditionally

It is often better to exit the program rather than proceeding with invalid input. You can do this conditionally using the built-in exit() function:

choice = input("Enter 1, 2 or 3: ")
if not choice.isdigit():
   exit(f"{choice!r} is not a valid number")
choice = int(choice)
if choice not in (1,2,3):
   exit(f"Unknown option {choice}")

items.title: If Statements
items.text: if statements let you branch out based on the outcome of a boolean test.

items.title: Code blocks
items.text:
Code blocks are a group of one or more statements that are meant to be executed as a unit. They are used to define the body of conditional statements, loops, functions and classes.

Python uses indentation to define code blocks and they have the following shape:

  • the block definition statement must end with a colon (:)
  • the block's body must be indented to the right by one space or more (4 spaces is the recommended amount). The indentation must be consistent for the entire block.
  • the block ends when the indentation returns to the previous level.

items.title: if — single branching
items.text:
Executes the block only if the test condition is True, and does nothing otherwise.

>>> temp = 32
>>> if temp > 30:
...    print("It's hot")
...    print("Drink water")
...
It's hot
Drint water

items.title: if - elif - else - multiple branching
items.text:
Evaluate multiple test conditions and execute the block of the first "true" branch. The else clause runs if no other branch evaluated to True.

>>> score = 75
>>> if score >= 90:
...    grade = "A"
... elif score >= 80:
...    grade = "B"
... elif score >= 70:
...    grade = "C"
... else:
...    grade = "F"
...
>>> print(grade) 
C

Order matters

Put the most specific / highest conditions first when there is overlap. In the previous example, if score >=70 were put first, everybody with a score greater than 70 would get a grade of "C", making the "A" and "B" grades unattainable!

items.title: Ternary operator
items.text:
You can use if - else to write expressions that return a value of any type based on a boolean expression

>>> height = int(input("Enter height in centimeters: "))
Enter height: 130
>>> "Tall" if height > 160 else "Short"
'Short'

items.title: Example
items.text:
# ticket.py
age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
if age < 0:
    print("Invalid age")
elif age < 5:
    print("Free")
elif age < 18 or age >= 65:
    print("Discounted: $8")
else:
    print("Full price: $12")

items.title: Testing facts about a string
items.text:
The str type in Python provides a variety of methods that test a given string for the presence of certain properties and return True or False. These methods can be useful in conditional expressions.

  • Check for the presence of a given prefix or set of prefixes or a given suffix or set of suffixes 
    >>> text = "the quick brown fox"
>>> text.startswith("a")
False
>>> text.startswith(("a", "the"))
True
>>> text.endswith("dog")
False
>>> text.endswith("x")
True
  • Predicates useful for input validation 
    >>> text = input("What is your age: ")
What is your age: 30
>>> text.isalpha()
False
>>> text.isalnum()
True
>>> text.isdigit()
True
>>> text.isnumeric()
True

items.title: Searching and replacing
items.text:
>>> text = "the quick brown fox"
>>> "quick" in text
True
>>> text.find("quick")
4
>>> text.find("lazy")
-1
>>> text.replace("quick", "lazy")
'the lazy brown fox'
>>> text.count("quick")
1

items.title: Splitting and joining
items.text:
>>> text = "\n      the quick brown fox"
>>> print(text)

    the quick brown fox
>>> text = text.strip()
>>> text.split()
['the', 'quick', 'brown', 'fox']
>>> text.split("quick")
['the', 'brown fox']
>>> '_'.join(text.split())
'the_quick_brown_fox'

items.title: f-strings
items.text:
It is common to build strings from values stored in variables. f-strings provide a convenient way to achieve this. 

>>> item = "oranges"
>>> price = 1.5
>>> quantity = 5
>>> print(f"You bought {quantity} {item}")
You bought 5 oranges
>>> print(f"Total: ${quantity * price:.2f}")
Total: $7.50

The :.2f in the previous example is a formatting specifier. It tells Python to format the value as a decimal number with two decimal places.

In addition to specifying the type and precision of a number, the Python formatting mini-language lets you customize other things such as width, alignment, padding, etc.

>>> amount = 50
>>> f"{amount:>5}"
'   50'
>>> f"{amount:<5}:
'50   '
>>> f"{amount:>5.2f}"
'50.00'
>>> f"{amount:*>5}"
'***50'
>>> f"{amount:*^5}"
'*50**'

items.title: Formatting columns of text
items.text:
# invoice.py
print("your invoice".upper().center(34))    # str also can center!
print()
print(f"{'Item':<10}{'Quantity':>9}{'Price':>6}{'Subtotal':>9}")
print("-" * 34)
print(f"{'Printer':<10}{1:>9}{45.99:>6.2f}{45.99:>9.2f}")
print(f"{'Cartridge':<10}{5:>9}{10.99:>6.2f}{5 * 10.99:>9.2f}")
print("-" * 34)
print(f"{f"${5 * 10.99 + 45.99}":>34}") # you can nest them!

Item       Quantity Price Subtotal
----------------------------------
Printer           1 45.99    45.99
Cartridge         5 10.99    54.95
----------------------------------
                           $100.94

items.title: Dictionaries & Sets
items.text:
A dictionary is a data structure that maps keys to values. It is one of the most common data structures in programming and it is used to look something up by name instead of position. It allows you to store related data such as a collection of inventory items with their prices or stock quantity.

A set allows you to store unique values and perform membership tests and compare groups.

Both sets and dictionaries are unordered, that is, there is no guarantee that, during iteration, members will appear in the same order in which they were added.

In this lesson, you will learn how to:

  • create mapping and set structures
  • add, update and delete dictionaries items
  • safely look up dictionary items
  • iterate over dictionaries
  • compare sets and perform other set operations

items.title: Key–value pairs
items.text:
A dictionary maps unique keys to values, as a list of key: value pairs inside a pair of braces:

prices = {"apple": 0.50, "bread": 2.00, "milk": 1.50}
user = {"name": "Alice", "age": 36, "admin": True}
empty = {}

Value lookups use keys rather than indices:

prices["apple"]        # ⇒ 0.5
user["name"]           # ⇒ 'Alice'
prices["banana"]       # KeyError

Keys are usually strings, but can be any immutable value (numbers, tuples). Values can be anything.

Keys cannot be repeated. Attempting to create an existing key simply overwrites the existing value.

items.title: Add, update, delete
items.text:
prices["banana"] = 0.30      # add a new pair
prices["apple"] = 0.55       # update an existing one
del prices["milk"]           # remove a pair
len(prices)                  # number of pairs
"bread" in prices            # ⇒ True

Use .update(dict) to update multiple keys at once, or a key that may be missing:

prices.update({'carrot': 0.20})                  # potentially missing key
prices.update({'milk': 1.75, 'banana': 0.40})   # multiple updates

items.title: Safe lookup with .get()
items.text:
Looking up a missing key raises KeyError. When in doubt, use .get() — it returns None (or an explicitly stated default) instead of crashing:

prices.get("apple")          # ⇒ 0.55
prices.get("mango")          # ⇒ None       (no error)
prices.get("mango", 0.0)     # ⇒ 0.0        (your default)

Use .setdefault(k, v) to set a default value for a key that may be missing before accessing it:

prices.setdefault('lemon', 0.0)

items.title: Looping over a dictionary
items.text:
There are different ways of iterating over a dictionary:

for key in prices:                   
    print(key, prices[key])

You can get both keys and values in one fell swoop:

for key, value in prices.items():
    print(f"{key}: ${value:.2f}")

Use .keys() to get only the keys as a list.

Use .values() to get only the values as a list.

This means you can calculate statistics on dictionaries using the functions that work on lists.

For example, the following gives you the sum of all prices:

total = sum(prices.values())

And the following finds the highest price:

highest = max(prices.values())

And the most expensive item:

most_expensive = max(prices, key=prices.get)    # ⇒ 'bread'

items.title: Grouping
items.text:
Where .get() and .setdefault() shine is when you want to build dictionaries dynamically as when tallying items in a collection or grouping items by category.

Suppose you have a list of candidates, where each candicate's occurrence match how many votes they got:

votes = ['alice', 'grace', 'grace', 'bob', 'alice', 'grace']
totals = {}
for vote in votes:
    totals[vote] = totals.get(vote, 0) + 1
print(totals.get('alice'))                    # → 2
print("The winner is", max(totals, key=totals.get))

Similarly, suppose you have a list of employee names alongside their job titles:

employees= [("alice", "developer"), ("grace", "developer"), ("Alan", "designer")]
by_title = {}
for name, title in employees:
    by_title.setdefault(title, []).append(name)
print(by_title.get('developer'))    # ⇒ ['alice', 'grace']

The .setdefault() call ensures that there is always a list to append to even for a key that has not been seen before.

items.title: Nesting
items.text:
Nested structures are frequently called for to solve various kinds of data processing problem. List of dictionaries are used for database records. Lists as values in dictionaries can be used, for example, to represent lists of students in a course. Nested dictionaries can be used to model configuration for a software package, and the list goes on.

users = {
    "alice":   {"age": 36, "roles": ["admin", "dev"]},
    "grace": {"age": 40, "roles": ["dev"]},
}
users["alice"]["age"]              # ⇒ 36
users["grace"]["roles"][0]         # ⇒ 'dev'
for name, info in users.items():
    print(f"{name} is {info['age']} with roles {info['roles']}")

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
8.1 — Write a small program to build a phone book.

Start with a dict of a few name: number pairs. Add one, update one, delete one, and add several entries in one step.

Then read a name from the user and look it up such that missing name prints "not found" instead of crashing.

8.2 — Write a small program that reads a line of text from the user and counts the number of times each individual word appears in the text. Then print the results to the screen.

8.3 — Write a program that takes a list of names and groups the names by their first letter and print the results to the screen.

8.4 — Given two sets of students in two courses, write a program to find students in both courses, students in only one of the courses, and the total number of students across both courses.

8.5 — Write a small program that reads a line of text from the user and reports how many distinct words (case-insentitive) appear in the text.

8.6 — Given a set of required files in a repository, write a program that scans a directory and report if any required files are missing or whether all requirements are met.

Required files: config.yml, app.py, Readme.md

8.7 — Given two sets of skills — what a job requires and what a candidate has — write a program that reports the match percentage (the ratio of required skills that a candidate possess to the total number of required skills), the missing skills, and any extra skills the candidate has.

8.8 — Given a dictionary mapping students with a list of scores each, write a program that reports each student's average and the class average.

8.9 — Given two dictionaries containing item: qty, write a program that builds a new dictionary summing quantities for items in either dictionary.

items.title: Sets
items.text:
A set stores unique values in no particular order. It can be created as a sequence of values within braces or using the set() constructor.

colors = {"red", "green", "blue"}
nums = set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3])
empty = set()

Basic operations:

"red" in colors           # ⇒ True   
len(nums)                 # ⇒ 3     
colors.add("yellow")      # add one
colors.discard("red")     # won't crash if absent

Sets can be used to deduplicate other collections:

names = ["ada", "grace", "ada", "alan", "grace"]
unique = set(names)              # ⇒ {'ada', 'grace', 'alan'}
count_unique = len(set(names))   # ⇒ 3

items.title: Set operations — comparing groups
items.text:
In addition to deduplication, sets are useful when you have groups of objects and need to compare them:

  • intersection (&): elements in both groups
  • union (|): elements in either group, i.e, all of them
  • difference (-): elements in a but not in b
  • symmetric difference (^): elements in exactly one group
  • subset (<=): whether all elements in a are also in b
a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
b = {3, 4, 5, 6}

a | b        # ⇒ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} 
a & b        # ⇒ {3, 4}            
a - b        # ⇒ {1, 2}           
a ^ b        # ⇒ {1, 2, 5, 6}    
a <= b       # ⇒ False

items.title: Example
items.text:
Suppose you have two blog posts, each with a set of tags. You may want to know all tags used across both posts, which tags appear in both posts, which tags appear in one post but not the other, and so on.

post1 = {"python", "beginner", "tutorial"}
post2 = {"python", "advanced", "tips"}
print("shared:", post1 & post2)          # ⇒ shared: {'python'}
print("all tags:", post1 | post2) 
print("only in post1:", post1 - post2)   # ⇒ only in post1: {'beginner', 'tutorial'}

items.title: Pitfalls & idioms
items.text:
• {} is an empty dictionary, not a set — use set() for an empty set.
  • Sets are unordered — indexing (s[0]) is not allowed. Convert to a list when you need order.
  • Sets accept only unique, hashable (i.e. immutable) items such as numbers, strings, and tuples
  • Use .discard() instead of .remove() to avoid KeyError

items.title: Errors and exceptions
items.text:
An exception is Python's way of reporting that something went wrong. When an operation cannot do what it was asked, it raises or throws an exception, and that exception propagates up through your program until it is caught by some exception handling code. If nothing catches it, the program stops and prints text explaining what happened, which we call a traceback.

This lesson is about how to plan for, and gracefully handle failures when they occur. You will learn:

  • What an exception is, and what happens when an exception is raised
  • How to handle expected failures with try / except, and how to catch specific failures in order to provide better feadback.
  • How to use else and finally
  • How to signal failure from your own functions with raise
  • Strategies for checking a function's arguments against expected values
  • How to exit cleanly when an error is fatal

items.title: The question this page answers
items.text:
You write a function. Someone — possibly you, next week — calls it with something unexpected: a negative number, an empty list, the string "12 " instead of 12, None. How much should the function check, and what should it do when a check fails?

There is no single answer, but there are four recognisable strategies, and choosing between them deliberately is most of the skill.

items.title: Strategy 1 — don't check, and document the contract
items.text:
The default, and the right choice more often than beginners expect:

def average(values):
    """Return the mean of a non-empty list of numbers."""
    return sum(values) / len(values)

No validation at all. If values is empty you get ZeroDivisionError; if it contains strings you get TypeError. In both cases Python's own message names the problem, and the traceback points at this function.

This is appropriate when:

  • The function is an internal helper called only by your own code.
  • Python's own error is already clear enough.
  • The caller has already validated — checking again is noise.

What makes it legitimate is the docstring. "A non-empty list of numbers" states the contract, so a caller who violates it has been told. Validation you skip is only acceptable if the requirement is written down.

This strategy fails when the error surfaces far away

average([]) crashing inside average is fine. A function that quietly returns None on bad input, and crashes three function calls later, is not — see the sentinel-value problem discussed earlier in this lesson.

items.title: Strategy 2 — check first, then raise (guard clauses)
items.text:
Validate at the top of the function and raise immediately if something is wrong. The checks come before any real work, so the function either fails on line 2 or runs to completion:

def average(values):
    """Return the mean of a list of numbers.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if `values` is empty.
    """
    if not values:
        raise ValueError("average() needs at least one value")
    return sum(values) / len(values)

These leading if ... raise lines are called guard clauses. The pattern scales to several conditions, each with its own message:

def book_room(nights, guests, capacity):
    if nights < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"nights must be at least 1, got {nights}")
    if guests < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"guests must be at least 1, got {guests}")
    if guests > capacity:
        raise ValueError(f"{guests} guests exceeds capacity of {capacity}")
    return nights * guests * 50

Three properties make this readable: every check is one line, every message names the offending value, and the actual work sits at the end with no nesting. Compare the same logic written with if/else:

def book_room(nights, guests, capacity):      # harder to follow
    if nights >= 1:
        if guests >= 1:
            if guests <= capacity:
                return nights * guests * 50
            else:
                ...

Guard clauses exist to avoid exactly that staircase.

Use this strategy when the function is a boundary: called with data from a user, a file, a command line, or another part of the system you do not control.

items.title: Strategy 3 — try the operation and handle the failure
items.text:
Rather than inspecting a value to predict whether an operation will work, attempt the operation and catch the failure. Python's conversion and lookup functions are already precise about what they reject, so this is often both shorter and more correct:

# checking first — long, and never quite complete
def to_number(text):
    if text.isdigit():               # rejects "-5", "3.5", " 7 "
        return int(text)
    return None

# attempting — handles every case int() handles, which is the real question
def to_number(text):
    try:
        return int(text)
    except ValueError:
        raise ValueError(f"not a whole number: {text!r}") from None

The two approaches have names worth knowing, because you will see them in other people's code and documentation:

  • Look before you leap — check the condition, then act (strategy 2).
  • Ask forgiveness, not permission — act, and handle the failure (strategy 3).

Python leans towards the second, and for file operations it is not merely a preference:

# a real bug — the file can disappear between the check and the open
if path.exists():
    with open(path) as f:
        data = f.read()

# correct — the only moment that matters is the moment you open it
try:
    with open(path) as f:
        data = f.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    data = ""

Any check of the filesystem is out of date the instant it returns. The open itself is the only reliable test.

from None suppresses the original exception

In the to_number example above, from None hides the internal invalid literal for int() message so the traceback shows only yours. Use it when your message is strictly more informative; use from e when the original detail still helps.

items.title: Strategy 4 — normalise before you validate
items.text:
Much "bad" input is merely untidy. Before rejecting a value, clean it:

def parse_answer(text):
    """Return True/False for a yes/no answer, raising ValueError otherwise."""
    answer = text.strip().lower()            # normalise first
    if answer in ("y", "yes", "true", "1"):
        return True
    if answer in ("n", "no", "false", "0"):
        return False
    raise ValueError(f"expected yes or no, got {text!r}")

" YES\n" is an acceptable answer typed by a real person; treating it as an error would be hostile. Strip whitespace, fold case, and convert types at the edge of your program, so everything inside works with clean values.

items.title: Choosing a strategy
Where validation belongs
items.text:
The strategy matters less than the location. Validate once, at the boundary, and trust the value afterwards:

user input  ─┐
file data   ─┼─► validate here ─► clean values ─► the rest of the program trusts them
argv        ─┘

Re-checking the same value in every function that touches it doubles the code and the number of places a message can disagree with reality. If parse_percentage guarantees 0–100, then grade_for(percentage) does not need to check again.

items.title: A reusable prompt helper
items.text:
Validation at the boundary is repetitive enough to be worth one function you keep. This one combines a retry loop, a conversion attempt, and a range guard:

def read_int(prompt, minimum=None, maximum=None):
    """Prompt until the user enters a whole number within the given bounds."""
    while True:
        text = input(prompt).strip()
        try:
            value = int(text)
        except ValueError:
            print(f"  '{text}' is not a whole number.")
            continue
        if minimum is not None and value < minimum:
            print(f"  must be at least {minimum}.")
            continue
        if maximum is not None and value > maximum:
            print(f"  must be at most {maximum}.")
            continue
        return value

age = read_int("Age: ", minimum=0, maximum=120)
sides = read_int("Number of dice: ", minimum=1)

Note what it does not do: it never raises. This function's whole job is to deal with a human at a keyboard, where the right response to bad input is to ask again. It is the place where "handle it" belongs, which is why every function behind it can simply assume a valid integer.

Two kinds of function, two kinds of error handling

Interactive functions talk to a user and should loop and re-prompt. Computational functions take values and return values; they should raise and let the caller decide. Keeping these separate — no input() inside a calculation, no re-prompting inside a parser — is what makes code testable: you can call parse_percentage("101") in a test, but you cannot test a function that stops and waits for someone to type.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
9.1 — Write a program, safe_divide.py, that reads two numbers from the user and prints the result of dividing the first by the second. Handle bad input (letters) and division by zero separately, with a different message for each. The program must not print a traceback for either, and must print "done" as its last line in every case.

9.2 — Write a function, read_int(prompt), that prompts the user to enter a number and returns it as an int. The function should use exception handling to catch any invalid input, repeated prompting the user until a whole number is entered.

9.3 — Extend the function in the previous question to read_int(prompt, minimum, maximum), such that it also keeps prompting the user until the entered input is within a given range.

9.4 — Write a program, wordcount.py, that takes a filename as a command-line argument and prints the number of lines and words in it. The program should use an exception handling approach to enforce the following constraints:

  • if no filename is supplied, the program prints usage: wordcount.py <file> and exits
  • if the file does not exist, the program prints Error: no such file <file> and exists
  • otherwise, the program prints the counts

9.5 — Write a program, average_file.py, which reads a file containing one number per line and prints the average. Some lines are blank or contain text. The program must:

  • skip unusable lines, reporting each one as line 7: skipping 'abc'
  • still print the average of the usable lines
  • print a clear message if the file has no usable numbers

9.6 — Write a command line tool called sales_report.py, that reads a CSV file of sales and prints a summary. The program should handle all failures gracefully while providing adequate feedback about any failure that occurs.

The CSV file looks like this (the last three rows are deliberately broken):

region,units,unit_price
West,12,9.99
East,5,24.50
North,,9.99
South,abc,9.99
West,3

Spec.

  1. The filename is provided as a command line argument. If not provided, print a usage line and and exit.
  2. Define a function, parse_row(fields), that takes one row as a list of strings and returns a tuple (region, units, unit_price) with the numbers converted. The function should raise ValueError with a suitable message naming the problem for the following cases:
    • too few fields
    • a non-numeric quantity or price
    • a negative quantity
    • an empty region.
  3. Define a function, load_sales(path), that opens the file and calls parse_row for each row (skipping the header row). Bad rows are skipped, counted, and reported by raising a suitable exception. If none of the rows were usable, it raised ValueError. The function should not handle missing file.
  4. Define a function, report(sales), that prints the total revenue, revenue per region (sorted highest-first), and the number of rows included.
  5. Define a fuction, main(). It handles missing argument, missing file, unreadable file, and the "no usable rows" case. For each of these cases, the function should print a suitable message and exit. On success, the function prints a final count of skipped rows if any.

items.title: Not every error can be recovered from
items.text:
Some failures have an obvious fallback. A missing config file? Use defaults. A bad line in a data file? Skip it and count it. A typo at a prompt? Ask again.

Others leave nothing sensible to do:

  • The input file the program exists to process is not there.
  • A required command-line argument was not given.
  • The data file is corrupt in a way that makes every later result meaningless.

For these, stopping is correct. What is not correct is stopping with a traceback, which tells the user about int() and line numbers in your code when the actual message they need is "no such file: sales.csv". A fatal error should produce:

  1. a short message saying what was wrong, on the error stream,
  2. a non-zero exit code, so other programs can tell it failed,
  3. no traceback.

items.title: sys.exit — stopping on purpose
items.text:
import sys

sys.exit()        # quit, reporting success (exit code 0)
sys.exit(0)       # the same, said explicitly
sys.exit(1)       # quit, reporting failure
sys.exit("no input file given")   # print the message to stderr, exit with code 1

By convention — one that every shell, scheduler, and CI system relies on — 0 means success and any non-zero value means failure. 1 is the general-purpose "it failed" code and is all you need; larger numbers are sometimes used to distinguish kinds of failure, which is useful only if you document them.

You can see the code your program returned from the shell:

$ python3 report.py missing.csv
report.py: no such file: missing.csv
$ echo $?
1

That echo $? matters more than it looks. It is how a scheduled task, a shell script, or a pipeline knows whether to carry on, and it is the main reason a script that fails must not exit 0.

exit() and quit() are not for scripts

The bare exit() and quit() you may have seen at the >>> prompt are conveniences added for interactive use. They can be absent when a program runs in other contexts. In a program file, use sys.exit().

items.title: Two output streams: stdout and stderr
items.text:
Every program has two output channels. Normal results go to stdout; errors and diagnostics go to stderr. print uses stdout unless told otherwise:

import sys

print("42 records processed")                      # stdout — the result
print("skipping line 7", file=sys.stderr)          # stderr — the commentary

Keeping them separate is what makes a script usable as part of something larger. The user can save the real output while still seeing the errors on screen:

$ python3 report.py data.csv > report.txt
skipping line 7

The warning appeared on the terminal; only the report went into the file. Had you printed the warning to stdout, it would be sitting in the middle of report.txt, corrupting it.

Rule of thumb: if it is the answer, print it; if it is about the program, send it to stderr.

items.title: A small die helper
items.text:
Message plus exit code is such a common pair that it is worth one function:

import sys

def die(message, code=1):
    """Print `message` to stderr and exit with `code` (non-zero = failure)."""
    print(f"error: {message}", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(code)

if len(sys.argv) < 2:
    die("usage: report.py <datafile>")

Now every fatal path in the program is one readable line, and the formatting of errors is consistent.

sys.exit raises an exception

sys.exit works by raising SystemExit, which is why finally blocks and with statements still run on the way out — files get closed properly. It is also why a bare except: can accidentally catch an attempted exit and prevent it. One more reason to catch specific exceptions.

items.title: Deciding at the top of the program
items.text:
The pieces now assemble into the standard shape for a script: functions raise, and main decides what is fatal.

import sys

def load_scores(path):
    """Return a list of (name, score). Raises FileNotFoundError or ValueError."""
    scores = []
    with open(path) as f:
        for number, line in enumerate(f, 1):
            name, _, raw = line.partition(",")
            try:
                scores.append((name.strip(), int(raw)))
            except ValueError:
                print(f"line {number}: skipping {line.strip()!r}", file=sys.stderr)
    if not scores:
        raise ValueError("no usable rows")
    return scores

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print("usage: report.py <datafile>", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    path = sys.argv[1]
    try:
        scores = load_scores(path)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"error: no such file: {path}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    except PermissionError:
        print(f"error: cannot read {path}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"error: {path}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    for name, score in sorted(scores, key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True):
        print(f"{name:20} {score:3}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Three things to notice:

  • load_scores contains no sys.exit. It handles what it can (a bad row) and raises what it cannot (an empty result). It stays callable from a test.
  • main contains every exit. One place in the program decides to stop, which means you can see all the ways it can fail by reading one function.
  • Bad rows go to stderr and the program continues; a missing file ends it. That distinction — recoverable or fatal — is a design decision, and it is made explicitly here rather than by accident.

items.title: Handling Ctrl-C
items.text:
When a user presses Ctrl-C, Python raises KeyboardInterrupt. Left alone it prints a traceback, which looks like a crash for what was a deliberate act. If your program runs long enough for anyone to interrupt it, say goodbye properly:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        main()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("\ninterrupted", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(130)            # the conventional code for "killed by Ctrl-C"

The \n moves past the ^C the terminal echoed. Code 130 is the shell convention; 1 is acceptable if you prefer not to explain the number.

Cleanup on the way out

If the program holds something that must be tidied — a half-written output file, a temporary directory — put the cleanup in a finally so it happens whether the program ended normally, crashed, or was interrupted.

items.title: The one acceptable broad handler
items.text:
Everything so far has insisted on catching specific exceptions. There is a single exception to that rule: a last-resort handler at the very top of a program, whose job is to turn an unanticipated crash into a readable message while still failing.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        main()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("\ninterrupted", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(130)
    except Exception as e:                       # last resort only
        print(f"unexpected error: {type(e).__name__}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

This is legitimate because it does not pretend the error did not happen: it names the exception type, prints the message, and exits non-zero. It is still a trade — you have given up the traceback that would have told you where — so while you are developing, leave it out. Add it when the program is finished and being used by someone who should not have to read Python internals.

What this must never become

except Exception:
    pass                     # or: print("something went wrong")

A handler that discards the error and carries on, or exits 0, converts a loud failure into wrong results that nobody notices. That is strictly worse than crashing.

items.title: Summary of the exit decision
items.text: Situation Response Bad value typed at a prompt Re-prompt (loop) Optional file missing Use a default, mention it on stderr One bad row in a data file Skip it, count it, report on stderr Required argument missing Usage message on stderr, sys.exit(1) Required input file missing or unreadable Message on stderr, sys.exit(1) Output cannot be written Message on stderr, sys.exit(1) Ctrl-C Short message, sys.exit(130) A bug in your own code Let it crash — you need the traceback

items.title: Raising an exception
items.text:
If your own code encounters something it cannot sensibly handle, raising an exception is often the right thing to do.

For example, when a function is passed an argument it can't process, raising an exception will ensure that clear feedback is received by the caller.

Consider a function for calculating the avarage of a list of scores:

def average(scores):
    """Return the mean of a list of scores."""
    return sum(values) / len(values)

What should the function do when an empty list is passed? You may let it fail and hope it is handled somewhere else, but it would be more proactive to validate the input and raise an exception explaining why the function is unable to proceed:

def average(scores):
    """Return the mean of a list of scores.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if `scores` is empty.
    """
    if not scores:
        raise ValueError("average() needs at least one score")
    return sum(scores) / len(scores)

The if followed by raise is called a guard clause. It prevents the function from proceeding unless passed expected values, providing clear feedback otherwise.

The syntax is straightforward. It is the raise keyword followed by the type of exception with a message (details) explaining what the problem is.

Sometimes, multiple potential failures may occur, each requiring its own explanation:

def book_room(nights, guests, capacity):
    if nights < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"nights must be at least 1, got {nights}")
    if guests < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"guests must be at least 1, got {guests}")
    if guests > capacity:
        raise ValueError(f"{guests} guests exceeds capacity of {capacity}")
    return nights * guests * 50

Raising exceptions is most useful for validating function arguments against expected values. It is therefore important to choose the type of exception that best describes what's wrong with the argument. Some of the most commonly raised exceptions when checking arguments are listed below:

Situation Raise A value is the right type but out of range or malformed ValueError The argument is the wrong type entirely TypeError A required file is missing FileNotFoundError

Consider a function for withdrawing money from your bank account. The function accepts two numeric arguments, but not all numerical values are validi or make sense:

  • You must withdraw a positive amount greater than zero
  • The withdrawn amount cannot exceed the available balance (depending on the type of account)
def withdraw(balance, amount):
    if not isinstance(amount, (int, float)):
        raise TypeError(f"amount must be a number, got {type(amount).__name__}")
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"amount must be positive, got {amount}")
    if amount > balance:
        raise ValueError(f"cannot withdraw {amount} from a balance of {balance}")
    return balance - amount

items.title: Handling fatal errors
items.text:
Sometimes there is not meaningful way of handling a particular failure. In such cases, terminating the program may be the best course of action. However, it is still important to ensure adequate feedback to the extent possible is provided:

"""report.py — Data processing utility

Process data file passed as a command line argument,
and generate a summarized report.

Example:
    python report.py grades.csv
"""
import sys

def main():
    path = sys.argv[1]
    try:
        with open(path, newline="") as f:
            ...
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"Error: no such file: {path}")
        sys.exit(1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        print("usage: report.py <datafile>")
        sys.exit(1)
    main()

$ python report.py missing.csv
Error: no such file: missing.csv

items.title: Why a function should raise
items.text:
So far exceptions have been something that happens to your code. They are also something your code can do deliberately. When a function is asked to do something it cannot do sensibly, raising an exception is how it says so.

Consider a function that should never receive a negative number:

def square_root(n):
    return n ** 0.5

>>> square_root(-9)
(1.8369701987210297e-16+3j)

That is a complex number, which is almost certainly not what the caller wanted, and nothing in the program will notice. Three responses are possible, and only one of them is good.

def square_root(n):
    if n < 0:
        print("negative!")       # 1. print and carry on
        return None

Printing is a dead end: the caller gets None and crashes later somewhere unrelated, and the message appears even if the caller was perfectly happy to handle the problem itself.

def square_root(n):
    if n < 0:
        return None              # 2. return a sentinel value
    return n ** 0.5

Returning None is better, but now every caller must remember to check, and a caller who forgets gets TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) several lines later, pointing at innocent code.

def square_root(n):
    if n < 0:                    # 3. raise — the right answer
        raise ValueError(f"cannot take the square root of {n}")
    return n ** 0.5

Now the problem is reported at the exact moment and place it occurred, it cannot be ignored by accident, and a caller who does want to handle it can:

try:
    print(square_root(value))
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"skipping: {e}")

items.title: The raise statement
items.text:
The syntax is raise followed by the exception type and a message in parentheses:

raise ValueError("amount must be positive")
raise KeyError("no such user")
raise FileNotFoundError("config.txt not found")

Like return, raise ends the function immediately — nothing after it in that function runs. Unlike return, it does not hand a value back; it starts the search for a handler described earlier in this lesson.

The message is for a human reading a traceback or a log, so make it useful:

# unhelpful
raise ValueError("bad input")

# helpful — says what was wrong, and with what value
raise ValueError(f"age must be between 0 and 120, got {age}")

Use !r for values that came from text

f"got {value!r}" shows the value the way Python would write it, so "42 " prints as '42 ' and you can see the stray space. Without !r it prints as 42 and looks fine. For anything derived from user input or a file, !r is the better default.

items.title: Choosing which exception to raise
items.text:
Pick the built-in whose meaning matches your problem. The caller catches by type, so the type is part of your function's contract.

Situation Raise A value is the right type but out of range or malformed ValueError The argument is the wrong type entirely TypeError A requested key or name does not exist KeyError An index is out of range IndexError A required file is missing FileNotFoundError The operation is fine but the program is in the wrong state for it RuntimeError A function exists but you have not written it yet NotImplementedError

ValueError covers the large majority of argument problems in beginner code. When in doubt between ValueError and TypeError, ask: would a different value of the same type have worked? If yes, it is a ValueError.

def withdraw(balance, amount):
    if not isinstance(amount, (int, float)):
        raise TypeError(f"amount must be a number, got {type(amount).__name__}")
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"amount must be positive, got {amount}")
    if amount > balance:
        raise ValueError(f"cannot withdraw {amount} from a balance of {balance}")
    return balance - amount

Why no custom exceptions here

Large programs define their own exception types (class ConfigError(Exception): ...) so callers can catch their failures specifically. That needs classes, which are out of scope for this course — and for scripts of the size you are writing, the built-ins are genuinely sufficient. The habit that transfers is choosing the type deliberately rather than defaulting to one.

items.title: assert is not for argument checking
items.text:
assert looks like a validation tool and is not one:

def withdraw(balance, amount):
    assert amount > 0, "amount must be positive"       # DON'T do this

Two reasons to avoid it here:

  1. Assertions can be switched off. Running python3 -O script.py removes every assert statement, and your validation silently disappears.
  2. It raises the wrong thing. AssertionError tells the caller "a programmer assumption broke", not "your argument was invalid".

Use assert for tests — stating what your own code should produce, as in assert to_celsius(212) == 100. Use raise for input that comes from outside your code.

items.title: Re-raising: handle part of a problem, pass the rest on
items.text:
Sometimes a function can do something useful about a failure — log it, clean up — but cannot decide what the program should do next. Catch it, do your part, then raise with no arguments to send the same exception onward:

def load_settings(path):      # assumes `import sys` at the top of the file
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            return parse(f.read())
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"settings file {path!r} is missing", file=sys.stderr)
        raise                    # same exception continues up to the caller

A bare raise inside an except block re-raises whatever was caught, keeping the original traceback intact. This is much better than raise FileNotFoundError(...), which would throw away the information about where the problem started.

items.title: Translating an exception into a clearer one
items.text:
Other times the exception you caught is technically accurate but unhelpful to your caller. Raise a different one with a better message, and use from e so the original is still recorded:

def read_port(path):
    """Return the port number stored in a one-line file."""
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            return int(f.read().strip())
    except ValueError as e:
        raise ValueError(f"{path} must contain a port number") from e

The traceback then shows both: your message, and below it "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception" with the original. You get a readable error without losing the detail.

Don't translate just to say less

Replacing a precise built-in message with a vague one of your own is a step backwards. Translate only when you can add information the original lacked — which file, which field, which line number.

items.title: Who raises and who catches
items.text:
The division of labour that keeps programs readable:

  • Raise low, catch high. Small functions that compute and convert should raise and not handle. The top of the program — the input loop, main() — handles.
  • A function should not catch an exception it cannot do anything about. If the only honest response is "tell someone", let it propagate; the caller is better placed.
  • Never swallow silently. except ValueError: pass throws away information. If the value really is skippable, say so in a comment or a message.
import sys

# parse_line raises; the loop decides to skip bad lines and report them
def parse_line(line):
    name, score = line.split(",")
    return name.strip(), int(score)

def load(path):
    records, bad = [], 0
    with open(path) as f:
        for number, line in enumerate(f, 1):
            try:
                records.append(parse_line(line))
            except ValueError:
                bad += 1
                print(f"line {number}: skipping {line.strip()!r}", file=sys.stderr)
    return records, bad

parse_line stays short and testable because it has no error handling at all. load is the layer that knows "one bad line should not kill the import", so the handler lives there. That separation is the whole point of letting exceptions travel.

items.title: Handling exceptions
items.text:
There are two types of failures in Python: Syntax errors and exceptions. Syntax errors cannot be handled while the program is running. In fact, they won't even let the program run. You must fix them before the program can run.

Exceptions are runtime errors. They occur while the program is running and will crash the program if not properly handled. Examples include attempting to read a file that does not exist, using the wrong value in conversions, etc.

number = int("hello")
print("this line will not run")

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "demo.py", line 1, in <module>
    number = int("hello")
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'hello'

The traceback is read bottom-up:

  • ValueError is the type of the exception — what went wrong.
  • invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'hello' is the message — the detail.
  • The filename and line number where the failure occurred.

items.title: The try statement
items.text:
To handle an exception, put the risky code in a try block and specify what to do in an except block:

try:
    number = int(input("Enter a whole number: "))
    print(f"{number} times two is {number * 2}")
except ValueError:
    print("Invalid input. Whole number expected")

print("the program continues")

Here is the flow:

  1. Python runs the body of try, statement by statement.
  2. If nothing goes wrong, the except block is skipped entirely.
  3. If a ValueError is raised anywhere in the try body, Python abandons the rest of the try block and jumps to the except block.
  4. Either way, execution continues after the whole statement — the program does not stop.

items.title: Catching a specific exception
items.text:
The previous code catches only ValueError failures. In this case, this is what you want, because an unforseen exception is usually a bug, and you wouldn't bugs to be silently swallowed.

Consider the following:

# BAD — hides everything
try:
    total = sum(scores) / len(scores)
except:
    print("something went wrong")

A number of things can happen:

  • scores is empty: you get ZeroDivisionError
  • You misspell one of the variables: you probably get NameError
  • scores is a dictionary: you get TypeError
  • Any number of other failures.

What you want is probably this:

# GOOD — names the expected failure
try:
    average = sum(scores) / len(scores)
except ZeroDivisionError:
    average = 0.0

items.title: Common exceptions
items.text:
Exception Raised when Example ValueError the type is right but the value is not usable int("abc"), float("") TypeError the operation makes no sense for that type "a" + 1, len(5) ZeroDivisionError dividing by zero total / count with count == 0 IndexError a sequence index is out of range items[5] with 3 items in items KeyError a missing dictionary key prices["banana"] FileNotFoundError the path does not exist open("missing.txt") KeyboardInterrupt the user pressed Ctrl-C any long-running loop NameError the name has never been assigned a typo in a variable name

Some of these may be bugs instead of genuine errors (NameError, IndexError, KeyError). If you find yourself frequently writing code to handle these, ask yourself if there is a genuine case for these type of failures to occur.

items.title: Handling several exceptions
items.text:
One operation can fail for different reasons. There are two ways you can approach this:

Separate handlers, when each failure needs a different response:

try:
    with open(path) as f:
        config = int(f.read().strip())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"No config at {path}; using the default.")
    config = 10
except ValueError:
    print(f"Expected a number, got a string; using the default.")
    config = 10

One handler for several types, when the response is the same — list the types in parentheses:

try:
    with open(path) as f:
        config = int(f.read().strip())
except (FileNotFoundError, ValueError):
    print(f"Could not read a number from {path}; using the default.")
    config = 10

Note that Python will run only the first except block that matches. So, order matters. Start with the most specific and end with the least specific.

items.title: Reading the exception itself with as
items.text:
Instead of supplying your own explanation, you can use the as keyword to capture the exception object itself and use its description instead.

try:
    number = int(user_text)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Bad input: {e}")

items.title: else — code that runs only when nothing failed
items.text:
An else block runs if the try block finished without raising an exception.

try:
    with open(path) as f:
        text = f.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"{path} is missing.")
else:
    # only reached when the read succeeded
    print(f"{len(text.splitlines())} lines read")

The else clause is not used often. We could have kept the print statement in the try block, but if it raised another exception such as a ValueError, it may be silently swallowed. In this case it won't because the except block is specific.

items.title: finally — cleanup
items.text:
A finally block always runs, regardless of whether an exception was raised or not, whether the exception was handled or not. It is useful when you need to release resources your code may have acquired in the try block.

try:
    data = risky_operation()
except ValueError:
    print("bad data")
finally:
    print("this always prints")

items.title: Propagation
items.text:
An exception is not confined to the function where it happened. If the function does have code to handle the exception, Python walks up the call tree until it finds a matching except. If not handler code is found, the program crashes and a traceback is printed.

def parse_age(text):
    return int(text)             # may raise ValueError

def load_person(text):
    return {"age": parse_age(text)}

try:
    person = load_person("abc")
except ValueError:               # caught here
    print("that age must be a number")

items.title: The retry loop
items.text:
Combining a while loop with try is a common way to handle interactive input:

while True:
    try:
        age = int(input("Enter age: "))
    except ValueError:
        print("Please enter a whole number.")
    else:
        break                    # valid input provided. Exit loop

print(f"You are {age}")

Here is the same code, but with valid range check too:

while True:
    try:
        age = int(input("Age: "))
    except ValueError:
        print("Please enter a whole number.")
        continue
    if 0 <= age <= 120:
        break
    print("Age must be between 0 and 120.")

items.title: When not to use try
items.text:
As pointed out before, some errors indicate bugs rather than genuine exceptions. An if statement may be more suitable for checking these types of errors:

# DON'T DO THIS
try:
    name = record["name"]
except KeyError:
    name = "unknown"

# DO THIS INSTEAD
name = record.get("name", "unknown")

# DON'T DO THIS
try:
    first = items[0]
except IndexError:
    first = None

# DO THIS INSTEAD
first = items[0] if items else None

items.title: Working with files
items.text:
Reading and writing files is one of the most common tasks programs do. Files allow programs to remember by keeping state across runs.

In this lesson you will learn:

  • How to open files for reading and writing
  • How to persist program state using files
  • How to use structured data formats such as csv or JSON

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
7.1 — Write a program, save_load.py, that opens a file in append mode and adds a timestamped line to the file. When the program starts, it reads the contents of the file and prints them. Then, it repetitively prompts the user to enter a line of text, writes the line and a timestamp to the file and asks the user if they want to continue.

7.2 — Write a program, count_lines.py, that takes a filename as a command line argument, and prints the number of lines, words, and characters (similar to Unix utility wc).

7.3 — Write a program, todo.py, a task management utility that remembers your tasks between runs by saving them to a file.

Spec.

  • Tasks are stored in tasks.json as a list of tuples, each like ("buy milk", false).
  • On start, load the tasks (empty list if the file doesn't exist)
  • Support these commands (via a menu loop):
    • add <text> — add a new task (not done).
    • list — show all tasks, numbered, with [x]/[ ] for done/not-done.
    • done <n> — mark task n as done.
    • remove <n> — delete task n.
    • quit — exit.
  • Save to tasks.json after any change, so the list persists.
  • Decompose into functions: load_tasks, save_tasks, add_task, mark_done, remove_task, show_tasks, and a main() that coordinates everything.

items.title: Reading a file
items.text:
The safest and most common way of opening a file for reading or wrinting is using the with statement, which closes the file automatically even if something goes wrong:

with open("notes.txt") as f:        # open for reading (the default)
    content = f.read()              # the WHOLE file as one string
print(content)

Usually you want it line by line, using a loop:

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    for line in f:                  # one line at a time
        print(line.rstrip())        # rstrip() removes the trailing newline character

You can also get all the lines in one go as a list:

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()           # ['first\n', 'second\n', ...]

Note that .readlines() preserves the newline characters. Use .rstrip() to get rid of the trailing newline.

items.title: Writing a file
items.text:
open() accepts a second argument called the mode. It is used to specify whether to open the file for reading ("r", the default), writing ("w") or appending ("a").

  • "r": the file must already exist, otherwise an error is thrown
  • "w": overwrites the file if it already exists, otherwise creates the file
  • "a": if the file exists, the pointer is moved to the end of the file
with open("out.txt", "w") as f:     # "w" = write (ERASES existing content!)
    f.write("first line\n")         # write() does NOT add a newline — you do
    f.write("second line\n")

with open("log.txt", "a") as f:     # "a" = append (add to the end)
    f.write("another entry\n")

Note that you can also use print() to write to a file, which also adds newlines for you:

with open("out.txt", "w") as f:
    print("first line", file=f)
    print("second line", file=f)

Writing to an existing file

"w" erases the file the moment you open it. Use "a" to add without losing existing contents.

items.title: The persistence pattern
items.text:
File editing requires loading the contents of the file when the program stars and saving the changes at the end.

def load(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return [line.rstrip() for line in f]

def save(path, items):
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        for item in items:
            f.write(item + "\n")    # add the newline back

items.title: CSV — rows and columns
items.text:
Comma-separated data (spreadsheets, exports) is common enough that the standard library has a module. 

import csv
with open("people.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    for row in reader:              # each row is a LIST of strings
        print(row[0], row[1])

with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["name", "age"])
    writer.writerow(["Ada", 36])

items.title: JSON — persisting whole data structures
items.text:
For collection data structures such as lists and mappings, JSON provides the best persistence format. It saves the whole structure to text and loads it back with types intact.

import json

def save_json(path, data):
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        json.dump(data, f, indent=2)    # write the structure to the file

def load_json(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return json.load(f)             # read it back as lists or dictionaries

save_json("state.json", {"tasks": ["a", "b"], "done": 3})
state = load_json("state.json")

items.title: Functions
items.text:
As programs start to grow in complexity, the ability to encapsulate pieces of logic under a name that can be invoked on demand becomes invaluable. Functions let you do just that, and can receive inputs (parameters) and produce a result (return). What makes functions particularly useful is their reuse; i.e. you defined them once and reuse them on demand. Perhaps more than code reuse, it is the idea of decomposition — breaking a big problem into small, independently testable pieces — that make functions so useful.

You have already used built-in functions such as print(), input(), exit(), and others. This module is about user-defined functions. At the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • use the def keyword to define your own functions
  • write functions that accept inputs (arguments)
  • write functions that produce values (return)
  • explain when to use positional, keyword and default arguments
  • write functions that call other functions (decomposition)
  • write functions that call themselves (recursion)

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
6.1 — Write two functions to_fahrenheit(c) and to_celsius(f) for converting between celsius and fahrenheit degrees respectively. The functions should return the converted value.

6.2 — Write a function, is_even(n), that test if a number is even and returns a Boolean. Use the function in an if statement to test a number read from the user and print whether it is even or not.

6.3 — Write a function, largest(), that takes one or more numbers and returns the largest. Do not use the built-in max(). Use it on different combination of inputs, including inputs containing ties.

6.4 — Write a function, greet(name, times=1), that prints the greeting times times (default once). Call it using different combination of arguments: default, positional and keyword arguments.

6.5 — Write a function, initials(full_name), that returns the initials, capitalized. Then write main() that reads a name from the user and prints their initials to the screen.

6.6 — Write a function, password_strength(pw), that takes a string and returns "weak", "medium", or "strong" based length and whether it contains a digit. However, if the password consists of only digits, it should be reported as "weak".

6.7 — Write a function, fibonacci(n), that returns the nth fibonacci number. Write another function, fibonacci_series(n) that uses fibonacci(n) and returns first n fibonacci numbers.

Hints
  • 6.3 — start largest = a; compare against b and c, updating; return largest.
  • 6.4 — a for _ in range(times): loop inside the function.
  • 6.5 — split the name into individual words, the take the first character in each word.
  • 6.6 — use any(c.isdigit() for c in pw) to check for the presence of digits.

items.title: Coding challenge — Unit converter

1. Write the following unit conversion functions are pure functions, each with a docstring and a return (no print inside):
    1. c_to_f

3. Kilometers to miles
