Goodbye!

items.title: Defining and calling functions
items.text:
A function packages statements under a name. You define it with def and run it by calling it with parentheses:

def greet():
    print("Hello!")
    print("Welcome.")

greet()          # call it — runs the body
greet()          # call again — reuse!

items.title: Parameters and arguments — inputs
items.text:
A parameter is a named input to the function specified in the definition. An argument is the value you pass when calling the function. They're matched left to right:

def greet(name):             # `name` is a parameter
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Ada")                 # "Ada" is the argument → Hello, Ada!
greet("Grace")               #                       → Hello, Grace!

You can specify multiple parameters:

def describe(name, age):
    print(f"{name} is {age} years old")

describe("Ada", 36)

We call these positional arguments (the default); that is, the first argument is assigned to the first parameter (name = "Ada"), the second argument assigned to the second parameter, and so on.

items.title: Returning values
items.text:
The return keyword is used to hands a value back to the caller so the program can use it.

def square(n):
    return n * n             # send the result back

result = square(5)           # result is now 25
print(result)                # ⇒ 25
print(square(3) + square(4)) # ⇒ 25   (use functions in expressions)

If a function does not explicitly return a value, None is returned.

Consider:

def square_bad(n):
    print(n * n)             # shows it, but doesn't return it 

x = square_bad(5)            # prints 25
print(x)                     # ⇒ None

A return also ends the function immediately:

def abs_value(n):
    if n < 0:
        return -n            # exits here
    return n                 # only reached when n >= 0

A function with no return (or a bare return) returns None.

items.title: Default parameters
items.text:
Sometimes it is useful to assign a default value to a parameter at definition time. This makes the parameter optional, meaning the argument may be left out when calling the function:

def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    print(f"{greeting}, {name}!")

greet("Ada")                 # ⇒ Hello, Ada!
greet("Ada", "Welcome")      # ⇒ Welcome, Ada!

Default parameters are also called optional parameters. When present, they must come after required parameters.

items.title: Keyword arguments — pass by name
items.text:
You can pass arguments by parameter name, in any order. This can be useful for functions that expect several inputs:

def order(item, qty, order_type="Delivery"):
    print(f"{qty}x {item}, {order_type}")

order("mug", 2)
order("mug", qty=2, order_type="Pickup")      # keyword — self-documenting
order(qty=3, item="pen")                      # order doesn't matter with keywords

order(2, item="mug")                          # ⇒ Error

If positional arguments are used, then ordering matters.

You can force a function to accept only keyword arguments:

def greet(*, name, greeting="Hello"):
    print(f"{greeting}, {name}!")

greet(name="Ada")               # ⇒ Hello, Ada!
greet("Ada")                    # ⇒ Error - only keyword arguments allowed

items.title: Docstrings — documenting a function
items.text:
It is recommended to document every function. If the first line of the body of a function is a triple-quoted string, help(fn) will prints it:

def celsius_to_f(c):
    """Convert a Celsius temperature to Fahrenheit."""
    return c * 9 / 5 + 32

For more complex function, it may be suitable to provide more details in a multi-line docstring, documenting things like expected inputs, return values, how to call the function, etc.

items.title: Scope — local vs. global
items.text:
Names created inside a function are local: they exist only during the call and are invisible outside:

def compute():
    x = 10           # local to compute
    return x

compute()
print(x)             # NameError: name 'x' is not defined

A function can read variables from the enclosing (global) scope:

tax_rate = 0.1                 # global
def price_with_tax(p):
    return p + p * tax_rate

Avoid relying on globals

Using global variables makes it difficult to predict the behavior of your functions. Instead, prefer using parameters and return values which keep functions self-contained and independently testable.

items.title: Variable number of arguments
items.text:
Consider this:

words = ["the", "quick", "brown", "fox"]
print(*words)       # ⇒ the quick brown fox

The built-in print() function accepts a variable number of arguments. If you have a list of words, you can unpack it into the function call using the *args syntax.

To define such a function, the same syntax is used:

def log(*messages, level="INFO"):
    for msg in messages:
        print(f"::{level}:: {msg}")

log("initializing volume", "checking system health", level="DEBUG")

items.title: Lambda functions
items.text:
If you function has a one line body, then it can be defined more concisely using lambda syntax. Supposed you need a function to test if a number is even. You can define it like this:

is_even = lambda x: x % 2 == 0

is_even(3)      # ⇒ False
is_even(6)      # ⇒ True

Lambda functions can be useful in functions that take other functions as arguments:

fruits = ["orange", "avocado", "pineapple", "apple", "banana"]

print(sorted(fruits))                           # ⇒ ['apple', 'avocado', 'banana', 'orange', 'pineapple']

print(sorted(fruits, key=lambda x: len(x)))     # ⇒ ['apple', 'banana', 'orange', 'avocado', 'pineapple']

items.title: Recursion
items.text:
Functions can call other functions. When a function calls itself, this is called recursion. Recursion is often deployed to solve problems that present smaller versions of themselves when broken down.

def factorial(n):
    if n < 0:
        return -1
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)

print(factorial(5))             # ⇒ 120

items.title: Decomposition
items.text:
Functions enable a style of programming where a complex task can be broken down into smaller tasks that are easier to solve. This works best when each function has a single responsibility.

Suppose you want to find the average daily temperature over a period of several days:

# avg_temperature.py

def read_temps(n):
    """Read n temperatures from the user, return them as a list."""
    temps = []
    for i in range(n):
        temps.append(float(input(f"temp {i+1}: ")))
    return temps

def average(values):
    """Return the mean of a non-empty list of numbers."""
    return sum(values) / len(values)

def main():
    temps = read_temps(3)
    print(f"Average: {average(temps):.1f}")

main()

Almost all programs are written like this. You define small functions, each solving one part of the problem, then compose them to solve the whole problem.

items.title: Getting Python
items.text: Before you can start writing programs, you need to install the Python interpreter on you machine.

items.title: Install Python
items.text:
You want Python 3.10 or newer (newer versions have friendlier error messages).

WindowsmacOSLinux

Get the Installer from the official Python website.

Add it to the system PATH

On the first installer screen, check "Add python.exe to PATH..

If you forget to do this, you will get an error when you try to run Python for the first time, and you will have to add it to the PATH manually.

brew install python, or use the installer from python.org

Python is almost certainly already there. Run python --version to check.

If not already installed, use your distro's package manager to install it.

Info

On some Linux distros, Python is invoked with python3 instead of python. Try which python and which python3 and if neither of those yields an answer, Python is probably not installed.

items.title: Install a code editor
items.text:
While you can write Python programs using any text editor, code editors provide a much better user experience. Some of the features you may want in a coded editor include:

  • Syntax highlighting: reveal the structure of your code using different colors
  • Automatic indentation: Python uses indentation as syntax and it is easy to forget or be inconsistent in how you indent your code. A good code editor takes care of that for you
  • Catch errors: you will make many mistakes while programming Python. A good code editor lets you know when that happens.

There are many code editors to choose from, but this course recommends Visual Studio Code from Microsoft. Get it from here: VS Code Download

Install Python extension in VS Code

In VS Code, go to Extensions tab, and search for "python". The official Microsoft Python extension is called ms-python.python. It has a Microsoft badge. Go ahead and install it.

The extension has features that makes it easier to write correct Python code. It should be pretty much the only extension you need.

items.title: Running Python
items.text: Python programs are instructions that are executed by an interpreter. The interpreter can be used interactively to execute instructions as you type them, or it can be used to execute instructions contained in a text file, a.k.a, a script.

items.title: The REPL — an interactive prompt for quick checks
items.text:
REPL stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop. It read Python expressions you type into it, evaluates them, prints the results to the screen and then waits for the next instruction.

Type python with no arguments into a terminal window. You will see these characters >>> printed on the screen, followed by a space. We call this a prompt and it is waiting for you to type something.

Try this:

>>> 2 + 3
5
>>> "hi" * 3
'hihihi'
>>> name = "Ada"
>>> name
'Ada'

Press Ctrl-D (macOS/Linux) or Ctrl-Z then Enter (Windows), or type exit(), to leave. Throughout the course, lines beginning with >>> mean "type this into the REPL" and the line under it is what the REPL echoes back.

items.title: Script files — for anything more than a line or two
items.text:
Real programs live in .py files. Create one and run it:

python3 hello.py

Where hello.py contains:

print("hello from a script")

hello from a script

Use print() if you want to see output from a script

The REPL evaluates what you type and prints the results immediately. A script does not - there you must call print(...) if you want to see output on the screen.

items.title: Create a home for your programs
items.text:
Make a folder for this course so nothing you try affects your existing files:

mkdir acit1515 && cd acit1515

Learn to use the terminal

mkdir and cd in the previous command create a folder and change into it respectively.

It is important to familiarize yourself with the terminal enough to be able to navigate the filesystem, create, open and delete files and folders and run commands. This is one of the first skills a programmer is expected to learn.

Also, learn where things are on your system. Make sure you know how to find where programs are installed, how to find your files, how to tell the type of a file - for example, Python scripts use the .py suffix. When you see such a file, you can immediately tell that it is a program intended to be processed by the Python interpreter. Similarly, when you see a .txt this tells you the file contains text, but it is not executable.

items.title: Getting help
items.text:
Python literally has a built-in help() function that exists to explain things. It doesn't explain everything, only things the interpreter knows. But it can be a quick way to look up information about Python language constructs and other Python objects.

Try this:

help(print)
help('while')       # for python keywords, surround them with quotes

For more detailed explanations, The Official Python Tutorial is a good place to start.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
1.1 — Write about_me.py that prints three lines: your name, your city, and the number of programming languages you know (as a number, not text).

1.2 - Write the same program as above, but this time to this instead:

  • ask the user to enter their name and store this in a variable
  • ask the user to enter their city and store this in a variable
  • ask the user their favorite programming language and store this in a variable
  • print this information to the screen

1.3 — Predict, then run: what does each line print? 

print(5 * 3)
print("5" * 3)
print("5" + "3")
print(5 + 3, "apples")

1.4 — The following script has a bug. Read the traceback, say which error types it is, and fix it: 

print("Balance:" + 250)

1.5 — Use print to draw a small box exactly like this, using string repetition ("*" * n) — not by typing 10 stars by hand:

**********
*        *
**********

items.title: Homework
items.text: H1.1 — Write receipt.py that prints a mock receipt: a title line, a line of dashes made with string repetition, two item lines, and a total. Use print's multiple-argument form so numbers and text mix cleanly.

items.title: Input and Output
items.text: A useful program typically processes some input and produces output. Many programs manipulate text as both input and output.

items.title: print()
items.text:
In Python, the built-in print() function can be used to print text to the screen.

>>> print('Hello World')
Hello World
>>> print(5)
5

You can pass more than one value to the print() function; we call these arguments. When you do so, print() will output them with a space between them.

>>> print("x", "y", "z")
x y z
>>> print("total:", 3 + 4)
total: 7

Two useful keyword options:

>>> print("a", "b", sep="-")        # (sep = what goes between arguments)
a-b
>>> print("no newline", end="")     # won't print a newline
no newline

items.title: input()
items.text:
The built-in input() function is used to collect text typed by the user into a terminal and makes it available for the program to use. The input ends when the user presses ENTER.

>>> input('Please enter your name: ')
Please enter your name: Ada
'Ada'

You will always want to store the input into a variable before you can use it.

>>> name = input('Please enter your name: ')
Please enter your name: Ada
>>> print(name)
Ada

items.title: How Python runs your program
items.text:
A program is a list of statements the Python interpreter carries out in order, one after another:

print("first")
print("second")
print("third")

first
second
third

That top-to-bottom flow is the default and can only be changed by flow control statements and errors.

items.title: Comments
items.text:
Anything after # on a line is a comment. Python skips it entirely; it's there to explain why:

# Convert the price to cents to avoid rounding problems.
price_cents = 1999        # $19.99 stored as an integer number of cents

Good comments explain intent, not the obvious.

  • x = x + 1 # add one to x: not a very useful comment
  • x = x + 1 # advance to the next customer: this carries actual information

items.title: Strings and numbers are different kinds of thing
items.text:
"42" (with quotes) is text; 42 (no quotes) is a number. They behave differently

>>> print(2 + 3)
5
>>> print("2" + "3")
23

Mixing them is an error, and a very common one:

>>> print("age: " + 30)
...
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
>>> print("age: ", 30)
age: 30

items.title: Reading error messages
items.text:
When Python can't run something, it stops and prints a traceback. A traceback tells you what happened and where.

Always start reading from the bottom. That's where the most instructive information is.

# boom.py

print("start")
print(10 / 0)       # boom 
print("never runs")

start
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "boom.py", line 4, in <module>
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

  • ZeroDivisionError: division by zero — what went wrong.
  • File "boom.py", line 4 — where.
  • start printed, never runs did not — Python stopped at the error.

Here are some of the most common errors:

Error Means Typical cause SyntaxError Python can't even parse the line missing ), missing quote NameError a name isn't defined typo, or used before assigned TypeError wrong kind of value "age" + 30

items.title: Worked examples
items.text:
# greet.py — a first real script
print("What this program does: greets the world three ways.")
print("Hello, world!")
print("Hello,", "world!")            # print joins with a space
print("Hel" + "lo" + ", world!")     # strings joined by hand
print("=" * 20)                      # ⇒ ==================== (repeat a string)

What this program does: greets the world three ways.
Hello, world!
Hello, world!
Hello, world!
====================

items.title: Sequences
items.text:
Many programs are written to process collections of data. Sequences are one of the most common collection data types in Python. This group include lists, tuples, and ranges. Sequences are ordered, meaning their elements can be accessed by index.

Some sequences are mutable, meaning they can grow and shrink. Lists in Python are mutable sequences.

Some sequences are immutable, meaning they cannot be modified once created. This group includes tuples and ranges.

Sequences are iterables, that is, you can loop over them to process each item individually.

At the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • create lists, tuples and ranges
  • mutate lists using the list type methods
  • slice sequences
  • iterate sequences
  • write simple list comprehensions

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
5.1 — Given the list nums = [5, 3, 9, 1, 7]. Write a program that prints its length, sum, max, min, and average. Then sort the list in ascending and descending order without losing the original order, and print the results.

5.2 — Write a program that reads numbers from the user until they enter an empty line, collecting them into a list. The program then prints the list, its total, and its average.

5.3 — Write a program that reads text from the user, splits the text it into words and prints the following:

  • the word count
  • the longest word
  • the list of words longer than 4 letters

5.4 — Write a program that reads a list of numbers from the user. Create a new list with the even numbers removed and then print both lists.

5.5 — Write a program stats.py that reads a list of numbers from the user. The program then calculates the count, sum, average, min, max and the median (sort then pick the middle, handling both even and odd lengths) and prints the results to the screen.

5.6 — Write a program dedupe.py that reads a list of numbers from the user and produces a new list without duplicates while preserving the original order. Print both lists to the screen.

5.7 — Write a program rotate.py that reads a list of numbers from the user and a rotation position k (an integer; must be less than the length of the list). The program then produces a new list from the input list rotated by k positions and prints both lists to the screen.

Examples:

  • [1,2,3,4] with k = 1 ⇒ [2,3, 4, 1]
  • [1,2,3,4] with k = 2 ⇒ [3,4,1,2]

5.8 — A perfect number is a number that is equal to the sum of its proper divisors (excluding the number itself). Write a program that reads a number from the user, finds its divisors and calculates their sum. The program then declares if the number is "perfect" or not.

Hints
  • 5.2 — check if the value returned by input() is empty and use break to end the loop
  • 5.4 — a list comprehension that filters on n % 2 != 0 would be perfect here
  • 5.5 — average and median are different. The median is the value literally in the middle after the list is sorted
  • 5.6 — build a new list, doing a membership check on each iteration before adding the number to the new list

items.title: for-loop
items.text:
Sequences are iterables, which means they naturally support for loop.

A for loop walks through the items of a sequence one item per iteration.

scores = [89, 49, 94]
for score in scores:
    print(score)

You don't manage a counter or an exit condition. The loop ends when the items run out, or is interrupted by a break statement.

If you only want to repeat an operation a given number of times, range() is enough:

# prompt the user for the password 3 times
password = 'secret'
for _ in range(3):
    if password == input('Please enter your password: '):
        print('Access granted')
        break
else:
    print('Access denied')

The else in the previous code snippet is not an error. It follows the for statement, not the if statement. That is, the body of that else clause will only run if the loop terminates normally, in this case, if the user fails to enter the correct password after 3 attempts.

Use enumerate() if you want the items positions:

names = ['Ada', 'Turing', 'Newman']
for pos, name in enumerate(names):
    print(f"{pos}: {name}")

Note that in the previous example, pos and name are assigned using unpacking.

The same can be achieved using range():

for pos in range(len(names)):
    print(f"{pos}: {names[pos]}")

As you can see, the enumerate() version is much cleaner.

Listing items of a sequence is not all that interesting. Instead, you often want to compute something from the sequence. This may include generating a new sequence, filtering, searching, aggregating, etc.

scores = [89, 49, 94, 50]
passing = []
for score in scores:
    if score >= 50:
        passing.append(score)

# count vowels in a string
text = "programming"
vowels = 0
for ch in text:
    if ch in "aeiou":
        vowels += 1
print(vowels)             # ⇒ 3

If the list contains only numeric values, the built-in functions such as min(), max(), sum(), and len() allow you to compute aggregates without needing a for loop.

scores = [89, 49, 94, 50]
avg = sum(scores) / len(scores)

items.title: break and continue
items.text:
These work just as they do for while loops:

# stop at the first negative number
for n in [3, 8, -1, 5]:
    if n < 0:
        break             # leave the loop now
    print(n)              # ⇒ 3  8

# skip blanks, process the rest
for line in ["a", "", "b"]:
    if line == "":
        continue          # skip to next item
    print(line)           # ⇒ a  b

items.title: List comprehensions
items.text:
A comprehension is a compact way to build a list by transforming or filtering another sequence. You can think of it as a shorthand for building a list using a loop.

# squares of 0..4
squares = [n * n for n in range(5)]          # ⇒ [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]

# with a filter
evens = [n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0] # ⇒ [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]

# transform 
names = ["ada", "grace"]
caps = [name.upper() for name in names]      # ⇒ ['ADA', 'GRACE']

Don't overdo it

Lists comprehensions shine best when they are kept simple. Start by writing the loop version and extract your list construction logic. If it needs more than one if or is getting too long, a regular loop is often the better idea.

items.title: Creating and indexing
items.text:
A list is written with square brackets. Lists can be empty or contain comma-separated item. Items can be any type and can even mixed:

scores = [88, 92, 79, 95]
names = ["Ada", "Grace", "Alan"]
mixed = ["Ada", 36, True]
empty = []

Lists can be indexed, concatenated and sliced exactly like strings. Indexes are 0-based:

scores[0]      # ⇒ 88     first
scores[-1]     # ⇒ 95     last
scores[1:3]    # ⇒ [92, 79]   a slice is a NEW list
len(scores)    # ⇒ 4

[2] + [3]      # ⇒ [2, 3]
[2] * 3        # ⇒ [2, 2, 2]

items.title: Mutating lists
items.text:
Unlike strings, you can change a list's contents without making a new one:

scores = [88, 92, 79]
scores[0] = 100          # replace an element
print(scores)            # ⇒ [100, 92, 79]

Lists can contain other lists:

matrix = [[1,2,3], [4,5,6], [7,8,9]]

The list type defines several methods that change a list in place:

nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums.append(4)           # add ONE item to the end     → [1, 2, 3, 4]
nums.insert(0, 9)        # insert at an index           → [9, 1, 2, 3, 4]
nums.extend([5, 6])      # add several from another list→ [9, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
nums.remove(9)           # remove first matching VALUE  → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
last = nums.pop()        # remove & RETURN the last     → last=6
first = nums.pop(0)      # remove & return by index     → first=1
nums.sort()              # sort IN PLACE (ascending)
nums.sort(reverse=True)  # descending
nums.reverse()           # reverse in place
nums.clear()             # empty it

Mutating methods don't return a value

Generally, methods that change a list's contents in place return None.

A common mistake is to mutate and re-bind a reference to a list:

nums = nums.append(4)

This will not have the expected outcome. The expression will throw away your list and store None instead.

The exception is .pop() which removes a value from the list and returns it.

Non-mutating alternatives

It is often recommended to avoid changing a list in place, but what alternatives are there?

  • concatenation: .append() and .extend() 
    nums = [1, 2, 3]    
nums + [4]                  # → [1, 2, 3, 4]
nums + [4,5,6]              # → [ 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 6]
  • slicing: .insert() 
    nums[:0] + [9] + nums[0:]   # → [9, 1, 2, 3]
  • non-mutating functions: non-mutating built-in functions for sorting and reversing lists: 
    nums = [4,3,6,2]
sorted(nums)                # → [2, 3, 4, 6]
sorted(nums, reverse=True)  # → [6, 4, 3, 2]
list(reversed(nums))        # → [2, 6, 3, 4]

items.title: Searching, couting, and aggregation
items.text:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
3 in nums               # → True
nums.count(2)           # number of occurrences of 2 in the list
nums.index(3)           # position of first occurrence of 3 in the list
sum(nums)               # ⇒ total (works only for lists of numbers)
min(nums)               # → 1
max(nums)               # → 3

items.title: Lists from strings and back
items.text:
text = 'the quick brown fox'
words = text.split()
print(len(words), "words")      # ⇒ 3 words

csv_header = ["Name", "Job Title", "Salary"]
';'.join(csv_header)

items.title: list gotchas
items.text:
• Aliasing

    a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a               # → b is not a new list, but an alias of a

b.append(4)
print(b)            # ⇒ [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(a)            # ⇒ [1, 2, 3, 4]

  • Copying

    nums = [1,2,3]
nums.copy()     # → [1,2,3]

    .copy() only copies references of list items, not their values. For lists that contain other lists, this can lead to subtle bugs:

    nums = [[1], [1], [1]]
copy = nums.copy()

id(nums[0]) == id(copy[0])      # → True

copy[0][0] = 5
print(copy)                     # → [[5], [1], [1]]
print(nums)                     # → [[5], [1], [1]]

    Watch out for this behavior too when you concatenate lists containing other lists:

    a = [[]]                 # a list containing an empty list
b = [[1]] 
c = a + b
print(c)                 # → [[], [1]]

c[0].append(3)
print(c)                 # → [[3], [1]]
print(a)                 # -> [[3]]

x = y = [[]]
x[0].append(1)
print(x)                 # → [[1]]
print(x)                 # → [[1]]

x = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
y = x * 2
y[1].clear()
print(y)                 # → [[1, 2, 3], [], [1, 2, 3], []]
print(x)                 # → [[1, 2, 3], []]

    This is why it is recommended to prefer creating a new list over changing a list in place

items.title: Range
items.text:
The built-in range() function is used to generate a sequence of numbers within a range. You specify an optional start position (the default is 0) and an end position. You can also specify an optional step (increment, decrement) parameter.

range() only stores those three parameters (start, end, step), and thus is very efficient in terms of memory footprint.

range() shows up a lot in for loops. It may be used to generate the values used in the processing, but more often than not its purpose is to control the number of iterations.

A range is not a list. If you want a list, you must consume it:

nums = range(2, 6)
list(nums)                  # → [2, 3, 4, 5]

list(range(0, 10, 2))       # → even numbers between 0 and 10
list(range(5, 0, -1))       # → countdown from 5

Ranges can be sliced just like lists:

nums = range(10)

nums[2:6]                   # → range(2, 6)
nums[::2]                   # → range(0, 10, 2)

Ranges are often used in for loops. See for loop

items.title: Tuples
items.text:
A tuple is an immutable sequence, i.e, a fixed group of values. Members of a tuple usually relate to each other in some way (coordinates, a record in a database table, ...).

A tuple looks like a list but with parentheses (or just commas), and it cannot be changed after creation:

point = (3, 4)
rgb = (255, 128, 0)
single = (42,)           # a one-item tuple NEEDS the trailing comma
also_a_tuple = 1, 2, 3   # parentheses optional — the commas make it

Tuples can be indexed and sliced just like lists:

point[0]         # ⇒ 3
point[0] = 9     # mutation is not allowed
len(point)       # ⇒ 2
3 in point       # ⇒ True

Tuple vs. list — when to use which?

  • Use a list when you want the collection to grow or shrink, or when you need to reorder the items.
  • Use a tuple for a fixed group where position has meaning and the value shouldn't change (a point, an RGB color, a database record, ...)

items.title: Packing and unpacking
items.text:
Packing is synonymous with creating a tuple, either by assigning it to a variable, or returning it from a function.

If you have a tuple, you can assign its items to multiple variables in one step. This is called unpacking:

point = (3, 4)
x, y = point             # x = 3, y = 4

Note that this is works for any sequence:

name, age, city = ("Ada", 36, "London")
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]     # first=1, rest=[2, 3, 4]

In an unpacking expression, * grabs any remaining items and returns them as a list.

You can swap two values by packing and unpacking in the same assignment statement:

a = 5
b = 6

a, b = b, c             # pack (b, a) then upack into a, b

The built-in enumerate() takes a sequence and returns a new list of tuples, each tuple containing the original item with its position:

names = ['Ada', 'Turing', 'Newman']
list(enumerate(names))                  # ⇒ [(0, 'Ada'), (1, 'Turing'), (2, 'Newman')]

The built-in zip() takes two or more sequences and return a new list of tuples, each tuple containing the items at the same position in the original lists:

scores = [67, 89, 90]
names = ['Alice', 'Eve', 'Bob']
list(zip(names, scores))            # ⇒ [('Alice', 67), ('Eve', 89), ('Bob', 90)]

If the input lists are not of the same length, the length of the resulting list is that of the shortest list.

items.title: Variables and data types
items.text:
Programs compute with values, remember them in variables, and combine them in expressions.

In this lesson, we look at:

  • rules of variables
  • how to work with text and numbers
  • some useful built-in functions

items.title: Converting between types
items.text:
Text from the keyboard (input()) always arrives as a string. To use user input in calculations, you must first convert it to numbers.

The built-in int() function takes a string, decimal or boolean (True or False) and tries to convert it into a integer.

float() does the same for decimals.

>>> year_of_birth = input("Please enter the year you were born: ")
Please enter the year you were born: 2006
>>> print("You were born", 2026 - int(year_of_birth), "years ago")
You were born 20 years ago

If int() is unable to convert the input, it produces a ValueError.

>>> int('abc')  # 'abc' does not represent any valid number in base-10
ValueError ...
>>> int('abc', 16)  # 'abc' is a valid hex number, i.e. base-16
2748
>>> int("3.5")  # does not allow a dot in the string. use `float()`
ValueError ...

Converting a decimal to an integer truncates the decimal part:

>>> int(3.5)
3

Python converts all operands of an arithmetic expression to float if any one operand is a decimal:

>>> 3 + 1.0
4.0

items.title: round() and abs()
items.text:
Use built-in round() to control the precision of decimal values:

>>> round(1 / 3)
0
>>> round(1 / 3, 2)
0.33

Use the built-in abs() to ensure a number is positive:

>>> abs(-7)
7
>>> abs(0.5)
0.5

items.title: ord and chr
items.text:
ord converts a character into its ASCII numeric value:

>>> ord('a')
97
>>> ord('A')
65

chr() converts in the opposite direction. So:

>>> print(chr(104) + chr(101) + chr(108) + chr(108) + chr(111))
hello

items.title: Examples
items.text:
# tip.py — split a restaurant bill
bill = 84.50
tip_rate = 0.18
people = 3

tip = bill * tip_rate           # 15.21
total = bill + tip              # 99.71
per_person = total / people     # 33.236666...

print("Tip:", tip)
print("Total:", total)
print("Each person pays:", per_person)
print("Rounded each:", round(per_person, 2))   # ⇒ 33.24  (round to 2 decimals)

# time_split.py — seconds into minutes and seconds, using // and %
seconds = 200
minutes = seconds // 60         # ⇒ 3
remaining = seconds % 60        # ⇒ 20
print(minutes, "min", remaining, "sec")     # ⇒ 3 min 20 sec

items.title: Excercises
items.text:
2.1 - Given the following restaurant bill:

  • bill: 84.50
  • tip rate: 0.18
  • Number of people: 3

Write a program (split-bill.py) that calculates how much each person will pay, rounding to 2 decimal points.

The program then computes the subtotal, adds 13% tax, and prints the subtotal, the tax, and the grand total, each rounded to 2 decimals.

The program should prompt the user to enter the number of minutes, store it in a variable, compute the split and print the value the user entered and the result of the conversion.

Then, using a single statement, swap the two variables.

Finally, print the "before" and "after" showing the values of a and b before and after the swap.

  • 2.3 — write 9/5 (true division) not 9//5 (which is 1!). This is a classic bug.
  • 2.5 — use multi-variable assignment syntax.

items.text:
H2.1 — Write change.py: given an integer number of cents (e.g. 287), print how many dollars and cents that is (2 dollars and 87 cents) using // and %.

The program should prompt the user for a number of cents above 100, store it in a variable, then compute the conversion and print the results.

H2.2 — Write powers.py that prints the first few powers of 2 (2**0 through 2**10). Use one print statement per line.

items.title: Numbers
items.text:
Numbers are one of the most useful data types in all of programming.

The two most commonly used number types are integers (int) and decimals (float).

Doing arithmetic:

>>> 7 + 2
9
>>> 7 - 2
5
>>> 7 * 2
14
>>> 7 / 2
3.5
>>> 7 // 2
3
>>> 7 % 2
1
>>> 7 ** 2
49

Division always produces a float

This is the case even in exact division:

>>> 10 / 2
5.0

n // m and n % m are complements of each other, and both produce integer results. The first produces the completed, whole part of the division. The other produces the remainder, or what's left over after the division.

0.1 + 0.2 is not equal to 0.3

Floating-point numbers cannot be represented exactly in Python.

Python always prints an approximation of the value stored by the machine. so, never compare two decimal values without rounding to the same decimal places first.

To learn more about this, read the Floating-point arithmetic module in the Official Python tutorial.

items.title: Precedence — the order of operations
items.text:
Python follows normal math order: ** first, then * / // %, then + -. Use parentheses whenever you're unsure or want to be clear:

>>> 2 + 3 * 4
14
>>> (2 + 3) * 4
20
>>> 2 ** 3 ** 2
512

Grouping is right-to-left

The last expression in the previous example may be surprising. ** groups right-to-left, meaning 3**2 is evaluated first.

When in doubt, parenthesize.

items.title: Strings
items.text:
In Python the type used to represent text is called string. You can use strings to provide feedback to the user during program execution or output logs from the program.

You can generate strings from other strings:

>>> firstname = "Ada"
>>> lastname = "Lovelace"
>>> fullname = firstname + " " + lastname
>>> print(fullname)
Ada Lovelace

You can convert most types to strings:

>>> age = str(25)
>>> print("You are " + age + " years old")
You are 25 years old

Without the str(25) conversion, the print() statement would have produced a TypeError.

Other ways to concatenate (join) strings:

>>> 'Hello' ' world'
'Hello world'
>>> ('Hello'
... ' world')
'Hello world'

Use pairs of triple single or double quotes for multi-line strings:

>>> html = """
<body>
    <h1>About</h1>
</body>
"""

Suppressing newline character in multi-line strings

When printed, the html variable will output a newline character at both ends of the string.

This is often not what you want. Use a \ to suppress a newline character anywhere in the string.

>>> html = """\
... <body>
...     <h1>About</h1>
... </body>"""

The special \ character is used to escape special characters such as quotes, non-printable characters and other characters that have meaning in the language (such as parentheses, braces, brackets, ...).

>>> "\"Watch out!\" she cried"
'"Watch out!" she cried'

Raw strings

There are times when you need to output the literal \. You can handle this in two ways:

  • escape the \: path="C:\\Program files\\Python314"
  • use raw strings: path=r"C:\Program files\Python314"

Uppercase and lowercase:

>>> 'python'.upper()
'PYTHON'
>>> 'PYTHON'.lower()
'python'

Get part of a string:

>>> lang = 'python'
>>> lang[0].upper + lang[1:]
'Python'
>>> lang[:-1] + lang[-1].upper()
'pythoN'

Indexing and slicing

lang[0] in the previous example is called indexing. This means retrieving the character at the given position in the string. Strings are sequences and their indexes start from 0.

The expression var[n:m] is called slicing. This means retrieving a substring starting at position n (inclusive) up to position m (exclusive).

Negative index values are permitted and they start at the end of the string.

items.title: Variables
items.text:
A variable is a name bound to a value with = (assignment). Read x = 5 as "let the name x refer to 5," not "x equals 5".

>>> price = 20
>>> quantity = 3
>>> total = price * quantity
>>> print(total)
60

A variable can be rebound, that is, it can be made to point to a different value, potentially of a different type.

>>> n = 10
>>> n = n + 1
>>> print(n)
11
>>> n = "now text"
>>> print(n)
now text

Right side first

In n = n + 1, Python evaluates n + 1 first, using the current value of n then makes n refer to the result. That is, the right hand side of an assignment statement is always evaluated first.

The value cannot be on the left-hand side of an assignment statement

The following is illegal in Python:

10 = n

The left-hand side of an assignment statement must always be an identifier, a.k.a variable name.

items.title: Naming rules & style
items.text:
• use letters, digits, and underscores
  • a variable name cannot start with a digit
  • variable names are case-sensitive (total and Total are different names)
  • style: lowercase with_underscores
  • style: descriptive. Prefer tax_rate over tr

items.title: Assignment shortcuts
items.text:
Multiple assignments on one line:

>>> x, y = 1, 2
>>> a = b = 0

Update and rebind:

>>> count = 0
>>> count += 5
>>> count -= 2
>>> print(count)
3

items.title: The while loop
items.text:
Computers are good at carrying out very simple instructions at a very high speed. At the same time, many programs consist of executing a set of instructions repeatedly. Examples include reading a file, listing the contents of a directory, searching, aggregating, etc.

In this lesson, we will look at one of the ways to do things repeatedly in a program: the while loop. At the end of the lesson, you will be able to:

  • Write a simple while loop
  • Understand the various ways to terminate a loop
  • Use break and continue to alter the flow of a loop
  • Use the accumulator pattern

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
Complete the following exercises using the while loop.

4.1 — Write a program that reads a number from user input, computes the average between 0 and that number rounded to two decimal places, and prints the results to the screen.

4.2 — Write a program that asks the user to guess a number between 1 and 10 and tells the user if their guess is correct or not.

With each run of the program, the secret number to guess is chosen randomly between 1 and 10 and stored in a variable.

The user should be allowed up to 5 guesses before the program terminates. If the user correctly guesses the secret number, the program prints "Correct!" and exits. If the guess if less than the secret number, the program prints "Too low" and lets the user guess again. If the guess is greater than the secret number, the program prints "Too high" and lets the user guess again.

After 5 incorrect guesses, the program print "Incorrect", reveal the secret number, and exists. Implement this using the loop's else clause.

4.3 — Write a program that prints the multiplication table for a number the user enters (7 x 1 = 7 … 7 x 10 = 70). Use string formatting to produce a clean and properly aligned output.

4.4 — Write a program that reads numbers until the user enters 0, then print how many they entered (excluding the 0) and their sum.

4.5 — Write a program that uses a while loop to count the digits in a string typed by the user.

4.6 — Write a program that prints a right triangle of stars of a height the user enters. For example, if the user enteres 3, the program would output:

*
**
***

4.7 — Write a program fizzbuzz.py. For numbers 1 to 30, print Fizz if divisible by 3, Buzz if by 5, FizzBuzz if by both, otherwise the number.

Hints
  • 4.1 — The average is the sum divided by total count
  • 4.2 — random.randint(1, 10) gives you a number between 1 and 10, all inclusive.
  • 4.5 — .isdigit() returns true if a string contains only digits. You can use it to check each individual character in the string. my_str[i] returns the character at position i, and len(my_str) gives you the length of the string. The last position in the string is len(my_str) - 1
  • 4.6 — use the end argument of print() to control when a new line is printed.
  • 4.7 — The order of checks is important here. For example, it is important to check if a number is divisible by both 3 and 5 before checking if it is divisible by either.

items.title: while — repeat while a condition holds
items.text:
While loops and if statements have a lot in common. They are both block statements, and they both use conditional evaluation to determine whether the body of the statement runs.

The while loop will repeatedly run its body until the continuation condition becomes false or the loop is interrupted by some other means.

count = 1
while count <= 3:
    print(count)
    count += 1          # ← MUST make progress toward the condition becoming false
print("done")

1
2
3
done

items.title: Two ways to terminate a loop
items.text:
• Make the continuation condition false in the loop's body. A while loop checks the continuation condition at the start of each run, meaning that if the condition is false from the start, the loop will never run, not even once. To make the continuation condition false, a controlling variable (count in the previous example) is used and it must be updated in the body of the loop in a way that will make the condition false eventually
  • Using break statement. See next section

The while loop is especially useful when you don't know in advance how many repetitions are required.

answer = ""
while answer != "quit":
    answer = input("Command (or 'quit'): ")
    print(f"you said: {answer}")

items.title: break
items.text:
The following two programs produce the same outcome using different strategies:

count = 0
while count <= 3:
    print(f"{count = }")
    count += 1

count = 0
while True:
    if count > 3:
        break
    print(f"{count = }")
    count += 1

The version with break is particularly useful in infinite loops, which is when the continuation condition cannot become false. This is the "loop until something happens" pattern. Here is another example:

while True:
    cmd = input("> ")
    if cmd == "quit":
        break
    print(f"Running {cmd}"

items.title: continue
items.text:
Sometimes you want to skip the loop's body and jump to the next iteration. The following program prints only odd numbers between 1 and 10:

current = 0
while current <= 10:
    if current % 2 == 0:
        current += 1
        continue
    print(current, " ", end="")
    current += 1
print()

Notice that we update current in two different places. This is a very common source of bugs. If current were not updated before continue, its value would never change and the continuation condition would remain true, leading to an infinite loop.

items.title: The else clause
items.text:
Just like if statements, while loops also can have an option else clause. This clause executes only if the loop terminates normally, meaning when the continuation condition becomes false. If the loop terminates due to a break statement, the else clause is not executed.

password = "secret"
count = 0
while count < 3:
    count += 1
    user_input = input("Enter your password: ")
    if user_input == password:
        print("Access granted!")
        break
    if count < 3:
        print(f"You have {3 - count} attempts left")
else:
    print("Allowed attempts exceeded. Access denied.")

If the user enters the correct password within 3 attempts, the else clause will never be executed.

items.title: The accumulator pattern
items.text:
It is common to carry out computations by accumulating values using a loop. This involves using a controlling variable, but instead of using it just to make the continuation condition false, the variable itself is the computation.

It has the following shape:

  • initialize the variable that will hold the final result
  • loop: each iteration is one step in the computation
  • update the variable with each iteration
  • use after: the computation is completed when the loop terminates

The following program calculates the sum of all even numbers between 0 and 10:

sum = 0
current = 0
while current <= 10:
    if current % 2 == 0:
        sum += current
    current += 1

Here's how to find the largest of some inputs:

biggest = 0
while True:
    user_input = input("Enter a number or 'q' to quit: ")
    if user_input == 'q':
        break
    n = int(user_input)
    if n > biggest:
        biggest = n
print(f"{biggest = }")

items.title: Nested loops
items.text:
Here's how to print a 3 x 3 table of numbers:

row = 1
while row < 4:
    col = 1
    while col < 4:
        print(f"{row * col:3}", end="")
        col += 1
    row += 1
    print()

Again, pay attention to how the controlling variables are initialized. col is initialized inside the outer loop before the inner loop, which essentially means it is re-initialized for each row.

Can you tell what would happen if col had been initialized before the outer loop instead?
